query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated temperature accelerates the formation of a thicker, Fe³⁺-rich passive film on Q235 steel, which suppresses subsequent corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposed Q235 steel, mechanically polished to remove native oxide films.
generation.intervention: Immersion in a 3.5% NaCl aqueous solution at 60 °C versus a control at 20 °C.
generation.conditions: Constant pH, dissolved oxygen level, and chloride concentration; static immersion for a fixed duration (e.g., 24–48 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The passive film composition and thickness, particularly an increased proportion of Fe2O3 or other Fe³⁺ compounds.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature enhances the kinetics of passivation, promoting the rapid formation of a dense and protective Fe3+-rich oxide layer that impedes further ion penetration and restricts electron transfer for corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) will show higher charge-transfer resistance (Rct) and thicker passive film features (confirmed via XPS/SEM) at 60 °C relative to the 20 °C reference, leading to lower corrosion current densities.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel immersed in the same chloride solution at room temperature (20 °C).
generation.boundary: Temperature is the sole variable; all other parameters (chloride concentration, pH, oxygen content) remain constant.
generation.uncertainty: Competing effects of increased ion mobility at higher temperature may partially counteract film protection; the exact film composition changes may vary with subtle environmental differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identically pre-treated Q235 steel samples and immerse them in 3.5% NaCl at 20 °C and 60 °C. After 24–48 hours, perform EIS, potentiodynamic polarization, and surface characterization (XPS, SEM) to assess passive film thickness and composition.
measurements: Passive film thickness and morphology via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 60 °C samples do not exhibit a statistically significant higher Rct, thicker/more protective oxide film (with increased Fe3+ content), or reduced corrosion current density relative to the 20 °C samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Rs is the internal resistance, that is, the resistance of the electrolyte and the working electrode itself. Rf is the Faraday resistance, including electron transfer resistance and substance exchange resistance, and Qf is the double electric layer potential, changing the electron configuration at the interface. R and Qdl are the resistors and capacitors of the passive film, respectively. Generally, it is believed that the high-frequency region of the electrochemical impedance spectrum of the rebar is controlled by the charge transfer process because the frequency changes too fast to allow for material transfer. It reflects the information on the charge transfer resistance of the rebar and the capacitance of the double

In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.

papers.title: Research on the Corrosion Behavior of Q235 Pipeline Steel in an Atmospheric Environment through Experiment.
papers.system: Q235 low‐carbon (pipeline) steel in a cyclic salt spray (accelerated atmospheric) environment
papers.approach: Accelerated corrosion testing with cyclic salt spray; weight loss measurements, morphology (SEM) and compositional (EDS) analysis; kinetic modeling of corrosion stages.
papers.findings: Identified four distinct stages of corrosion: an initial stage with slow weight loss due to effective passivation film formation, followed by a rapid increase (passivation film rupture and exposure to aggressive ions such as H+ and Cl−), a transitional stage with slight slowing as a loose rust layer develops, and finally a stage where corrosion kinetics stabilize with a lower weight loss exponent.
papers.mechanism: The initially formed passivation film delays corrosion but its eventual rupture exposes the substrate to aggressive environmental species. Subsequently, the formation of a rust layer provides partial protection, leading to a deceleration in corrosion rate over time.

papers.title: Electrochemical corrosion behaviour of four low-carbon steels in saline soil.
papers.system: Q235 steel (along with X65, X70, X80) embedded in natural saline soil
papers.approach: Electrochemical testing including open circuit potential (OCP), potentiodynamic polarization, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), combined with SEM, EDS and XRD to assess corrosion morphology and product composition.
papers.findings: Found that Q235 steel experiences localized oxygen absorption corrosion controlled primarily by mass transfer, with the corrosion process being more severe compared to higher grade steels due to differences in elemental composition. The corrosion product film was less uniform and compact, leaving Q235 particularly susceptible.
papers.mechanism: Corrosion in Q235 is predominantly governed by the diffusion (mass transfer) of aggressive ions (e.g., Cl−) to the steel surface rather than purely by charge transfer, resulting in rapid breakdown of the passivation layer and localized pitting.

papers.title: The Effect of Temperatures on the Passivation Behavior of Q235 Steel in the Simulated Concrete Pore Solution.
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel in simulated concrete pore solution at 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C
papers.approach: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), potentiodynamic polarization, Mott–Schottky analysis and temperature-controlled immersion tests to study passivation kinetics and film characteristics.
papers.findings: Demonstrated that the passivation process of Q235 steel is biphasic—a rapid passivation stage within the first 24 hours followed by a stable phase—and that elevated temperatures accelerate passive film formation. At higher temperatures, the passive film shows increased thickness and a higher proportion of Fe3+-rich compounds (e.g., Fe2O3), leading to improved corrosion resistance.
papers.mechanism: Temperature accelerates the growth rate of the passive film and influences its composition (favoring the formation of more stable Fe3+ oxides), which enhances the barrier properties against corrosive media. The enhanced film reduces further ion transfer at the metal interface.

papers.title: Corrosion of Q235 Carbon Steel in Seawater Containing Mariprofundus ferrooxydans and Thalassospira sp.
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel immersed in seawater with and without microbial consortia
papers.approach: Combined weight loss measurements, open circuit potential (OCP) tracking, SEM imaging, EIS, and surface composition analysis (EDS, XPS) to assess microbial impacts.
papers.findings: Showed that the presence of iron-oxidizing and iron-reducing bacteria leads to the formation of a heterogeneous biofilm, which disrupts uniform passivation and promotes localized pitting corrosion. Bacterial adhesion alters the electrochemical environment at the interface, yielding faster degradation compared to sterile conditions.
papers.mechanism: Microbial biofilms change the interfacial chemistry by either directly attacking the passivation film or creating differential aeration cells that lead to localized breakdown and accelerated pitting corrosion.

papers.title: Inhibition of Q235 Carbon Steel by Calcium Lignosulfonate and Sodium Molybdate in Carbonated Concrete Pore Solution.
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel in carbonated concrete pore solution with organic/inorganic inhibitor system
papers.approach: Electrochemical methods including cyclic potentiodynamic polarization and EIS were employed to study the effect of inhibitor compounds on the formation and stability of the passive film on Q235 steel. Pre-filming time effects were also assessed.
papers.findings: The combined use of calcium lignosulfonate and sodium molybdate enhanced the formation of a more protective composite passivation film. This film demonstrated better inhibition of both general and pitting corrosion, as reflected in increased polarization resistance and decreased double-layer capacitance. However, once pitting initiated, the inhibitors were less effective at halting pit growth.
papers.mechanism: The inhibitors work through competitive adsorption with aggressive ions (e.g., Cl−) and by promoting the transformation and stabilization of the passive film (e.g., transforming FeOOH to more protective Fe2O3), thereby delaying the onset of localized corrosion.

established: Q235 steel initially forms a passivation film that can temporarily slow corrosion progression.
Environmental aggressors (such as chloride ions, sulfate, and microbial biofilms) eventually compromise the passivation film, leading to localized pitting and accelerated corrosion.
Temperature has a marked effect on passivation kinetics, with higher temperatures accelerating the formation and altering the composition of the protective film.
Electrochemical techniques (EIS, OCP, potentiodynamic polarization) reliably reveal the transition between passivation-dominated and corrosion-dominated regimes.

mechanisms: Passivation film formation and its eventual breakdown under aggressive chemical exposure.

disagreements: There is some divergence over whether corrosion in Q235 steel is predominantly controlled by mass transfer (as seen in saline soil) or via charge transfer processes (noted in more alloyed steels).
Studies using inhibitors report that while the outer layer of the passive film can be stabilized, there is disagreement on the long-term suppression effectiveness once pitting initiates.
open_questions: Which factor—passivation film stability, aggressive ion diffusivity, or microbial activity—is the dominant trigger for the transition from protective passivation to active corrosion in pre-exposed Q235 steel?
How do ambient temperature changes, in the absence of other variables, modulate the balance between protective film formation and film breakdown on Q235 steel?
What is the precise behavior of the passive film under strictly controlled environmental conditions, and how does its composition and structure change prior to pitting initiation?
opportunities: Design a controlled study that isolates temperature as the sole variable by testing Q235 steel in a simulated aggressive environment (e.g., chloride-containing solution) at room temperature versus elevated temperatures (e.g., 40 °C and 60 °C) with all other conditions (pH, ionic strength, oxygen content) held constant.

Utilize in situ electrochemical measurements (EIS, OCP, and potentiodynamic polarization) combined with real-time surface analytical techniques (such as Raman or XPS) to directly correlate passivation film evolution with corrosion onset.

Investigate the interplay between passivation film composition (Fe2O3 versus other oxides) and its degradation kinetics under varied thermal conditions, aiming to decisively falsify hypotheses that attribute corrosion onset solely to environmental ion attack.

directions.direction: Investigate temperature‐dependent passivation kinetics and film composition evolution.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses how temperature affects the formation and composition of the protective passive film on pre-exposed Q235. The evidence (e.g., PMC9867134) supports the idea that higher temperature leads to thicker, Fe³⁺‐rich films, and the study is feasible via controlled immersion tests with electrochemical and surface analysis.

directions.direction: Examine the role of aggressive ion (chloride) diffusion under varied temperatures in initiating passivation film rupture.
directions.assessment: Directly tests whether enhanced ion diffusivity at elevated temperatures accelerates the breakdown of the passive film. Prior work (e.g., PMC9302071) indicates mass‐transfer effects in Q235 corrosion and offers measurable parameters via potentiodynamic polarization and EIS. Feasible with well‐controlled chloride solutions.

directions.direction: Assess the effect of thermal cycling and induced mechanical stress on passive film integrity and subsequent localized corrosion.
directions.assessment: Addresses the possibility that repeated temperature cycling induces micro-cracks at microstructural defects that serve as nucleation sites for pitting corrosion. Though indirect in past studies, it is mechanistically plausible and can be isolated using SEM and electrochemical techniques.

directions.direction: Determine if corrosion mechanism control shifts from mass-transfer to charge-transfer kinetics with temperature change.
directions.assessment: Proposes that at room temperature Q235 exhibits mass-transfer control while elevated temperatures enhance charge-transfer kinetics. Evidence from EIS and OCP measurements (e.g., PMC9782650 and PMC9302071) supports such mechanistic shifts. The hypothesis is testable via frequency-resolved EIS studies.
